title: Course Introduction
analogy: A component is a reusable recipe; props are its ingredients and state is the changing order ticket.

lessons.title: Think in user interfaces

notes.title: What React is and what it solves
notes.text: React describes a view from data. You compose functions that return UI instead of manually coordinating many DOM edits. It is a library, so you still choose routing and data tools.

notes.title: React versus vanilla JavaScript
notes.text: Both run JavaScript. Vanilla code can update textContent directly; React owns the DOM under its root and reconciles component output. A tiny static page may not need React.

notes.title: React versus React Native
notes.text: React DOM renders browser elements such as button. React Native uses native platform primitives such as View. Component thinking transfers; markup and platform APIs do not.

notes.text: Predict output before running an example. Change one input, explain the result, then rebuild from memory. Debugging your own mistake teaches more than copying a finished component.

notes.title: Self-assessment
notes.text: Browser progress records completion, not mastery. Revisit missed questions and build a project without looking at its solution. Keep notes about what you misunderstood.

notes.title: DOM and browser rendering

lessons.title: Connect browser and server

notes.title: JavaScript execution in browsers
notes.text: Scripts execute on the main thread unless explicitly moved to a worker. Long synchronous tasks delay input and rendering. Modules have their own scope.

notes.title: HTTP basics
notes.text: A request has a method, URL, headers, and possibly a body. A response has a status, headers, and body. GET reads; POST commonly creates. A 404 is an HTTP response, not a network rejection.

notes.title: Client-server architecture
notes.text: The browser presents UI and sends requests. A server controls trusted data and authorization. A static React bundle cannot keep secrets or enforce permissions.

notes.text: Use Elements for DOM/CSS, Console for errors, Network for requests, and Sources for breakpoints. Inspect the first meaningful error before changing unrelated code.

notes.title: Git and GitHub basics
notes.text: Git records local snapshots; GitHub hosts repositories and review workflows. Stage intentional changes, inspect the diff, commit a focused change, and propose it through a pull request.

notes.title: Debugging workflow
notes.text: Reproduce a failure, reduce the inputs, inspect values, make one correction, and retest the original case. Version control preserves a known working state.

title: Modern JavaScript for React
analogy: A function is a small machine: inputs go in, a value comes out; a closure also remembers its surrounding workbench.

lessons.title: Values, functions, and immutable data

notes.title: let, const, and scope
notes.text: let and const are block-scoped. const prevents rebinding, not object mutation. Use const by default and let when the binding changes.

notes.title: Primitive and reference values
notes.text: Primitives compare by value. Objects compare by identity; two identical object literals are different references. This matters when React compares dependencies.

notes.title: Functions and arrow functions
notes.text: Functions accept parameters and return results. Arrow functions capture lexical this; they do not create their own this binding. Keep rendering calculations pure.

notes.title: Arrays and objects
notes.text: Arrays represent ordered collections; objects group named fields. Destructuring extracts values. Spread copies one level; rest collects remaining values. Nested data still needs explicit copies.

notes.title: Template literals, optional chaining, and nullish coalescing
notes.text: Backticks interpolate expressions. ?. stops property access for null/undefined. ?? defaults only null/undefined, preserving valid 0 and empty strings.

lessons.output: Maya: 0 Maya: 5 0
lessons.why: React relies on clear inputs and new values for predictable updates; JavaScript identity rules explain why mutation is risky.
lessons.internals: Spread allocates a new outer object. Properties still point at the same nested references unless copied. ?? tests absence, not truthiness.
lessons.mistake: Incorrect: const next = learner; next.score = 5 changes the original. Correct: create a new object with a copied spread.
lessons.exercise: Update an address.city without mutating the learner. Independently write a function that formats a missing score as Not graded while keeping 0.

lessons.title: Transform collections and modules

notes.title: map, filter, reduce, find, and some
notes.text: map returns one result per item; filter selects items; reduce accumulates; find returns the first match or undefined; some returns a boolean. Choose the operation matching the question.

notes.title: Destructuring and spread in collections
notes.text: Destructure callback parameters for readability. Copy before a mutating sort, or use toSorted where supported. Never mutate a state array with push or sort in render.

notes.title: Modules and imports/exports (ES modules)
notes.text: Named exports use matching import names; a default export has one primary value. Use explicit module boundaries to isolate pure data operations. Import declarations are resolved by the module graph.

notes.title: Essential JavaScript interview questions
notes.text: Explain why map is not for side effects, why [] !== [], and why a shallow copy does not isolate nested objects. Demonstrate rather than memorize.

lessons.why: Collection transformations let a list view remain a direct calculation from its source data.
lessons.internals: These methods call your callback for each visited element. filter and map return new arrays, but their object elements can still be shared references.
lessons.mistake: Incorrect: students.sort(...) on state mutates the source. Correct: [...students].sort(...) or students.toSorted(...).
lessons.exercise: Return sorted IDs of students scoring at least 6. Independently export the function from selectors.js and import it in another module.

lessons.title: Closures, callbacks, and async work

notes.title: Closures and lexical scope
notes.text: A function can access bindings from where it was created. React event handlers and Effects close over a particular render; they do not magically read later state.

notes.title: Callbacks
notes.text: Passing a function lets another operation call it later. Passing save is different from invoking save(). Error-first callbacks and Promise callbacks have different contracts.

notes.title: Promises and async/await
notes.text: A Promise represents eventual settlement. async functions always return Promises. try/catch around an awaited call handles rejection. Parallel independent requests can use Promise.all.

notes.title: Fetch API and error handling
notes.text: Check response.ok, parse JSON, then validate the shape. Cancel irrelevant work with AbortController. A successful HTTP response can still contain invalid data.

notes.title: Immutability and React use case
notes.text: Use a functional state updater when delayed work needs the latest previous value. Avoid closing over an old count when queueing increments.

lessons.output: 1 2, followed asynchronously by 42.
lessons.why: Closures connect JavaScript function behavior to stale-state bugs in React.
lessons.internals: The returned function retains access to the lexical count binding. Promise callbacks run after the current synchronous stack finishes.
lessons.mistake: A try/catch cannot catch a Promise rejection if you forget to await or return the Promise within that chain.
lessons.exercise: Create two counters and prove their state is independent. Independently wrap a rejecting async function in try/catch.
lessons.question: What does an async function return?

notes.title: package.json and scripts
notes.text: Scripts name local tool commands. Dependencies are runtime imports; devDependencies support builds and tests. Both are needed when building from source.

notes.title: Development server
notes.text: Vite serves source modules and updates edited modules during development. StrictMode may repeat development work to expose missing cleanup and impure renders.

notes.title: Common installation errors

title: JSX and Components
analogy: JSX is a recipe for a tree of UI elements, not a string of HTML.

lessons.title: Write JSX expressions

notes.title: JSX syntax
notes.text: JSX is transformed JavaScript syntax. Return one enclosing element or a Fragment. Close all tags. It does not run in a plain browser console without transformation.

notes.title: Expressions in JSX
notes.text: Curly braces embed expressions, such as a variable or function result. Statements such as if and for belong outside the returned JSX.

notes.title: JSX attributes
notes.text: Use className, htmlFor, and camelCase DOM props such as onClick. aria-* and data-* retain hyphens. Inline style receives an object.

notes.title: Component naming
notes.text: Custom component names start with a capital letter. Lowercase names refer to browser elements. Name components for their domain responsibility.

notes.title: Functional components
notes.text: A component is a function returning renderable output. Define it at module scope so its identity remains stable. Do not call Hooks from ordinary utility functions.

notes.title: Component composition and Fragment syntax
notes.text: Combine components as children to form larger views. A Fragment groups siblings without adding a wrapper DOM element.

title: Props and Data Flow
analogy: Props are a delivery envelope from a parent; the receiving component reads it without rewriting its contents.

lessons.title: Pass and destructure props

notes.title: What props are
notes.text: Props are the inputs a parent supplies to a component. They can include strings, numbers, arrays, objects, and functions. Treat them as read-only snapshots.

notes.title: Passing values
notes.text: Quoted attributes pass strings. Curly braces pass JavaScript values, so count={3} is numeric while count="3" is a string.

notes.title: Destructuring props and default values
notes.text: Destructure in the parameter list for a clear API. A default parameter is used for undefined or missing values, not null.

lessons.why: Props make one implementation useful for many records without copying markup.
lessons.internals: Each parent render computes child props. Updating a parent value supplies a new snapshot; the child must not mutate its input object.

lessons.title: Use children for flexible composition

notes.title: Children and composition
notes.text: The children prop contains nested JSX. A layout component can provide structure without knowing which content it wraps.

notes.title: Reusable component design
notes.text: Expose the few inputs callers need. Use meaningful names like title and onSave rather than many unrelated boolean switches. Keep domain rules outside generic visual wrappers.

notes.title: One-way data flow
notes.text: Data travels down; callbacks communicate an intent upward. The parent decides whether and how to change shared data.

lessons.output: A titled panel containing the supplied paragraph.
lessons.why: Composition avoids duplicating wrappers while preserving flexibility for their contents.
lessons.internals: children is an ordinary prop with renderable values. Wrapping content does not require cloning or mutating child elements.

lessons.exercise: Add a footer prop to Panel. Independently compose a confirmation panel with a button callback.

lessons.title: Choose an owner for changing data

notes.title: Props versus state
notes.text: Props arrive from a parent; state belongs to the component that owns the changing value. A child may derive display values from props without storing another copy.

notes.title: Common mistakes
notes.text: Copying a prop into state only initializes it; later prop changes do not automatically synchronize that state. Use a controlled API or a deliberate reset when needed.

notes.title: Data-flow design
notes.text: Keep the smallest authoritative state. For a selected product, store its ID and derive the product from the current list; this avoids stale duplicate records.

lessons.why: A single source of truth prevents multiple copies of the same information drifting apart.
lessons.internals: Derived values recalculate during render. There is no need for an Effect to multiply two props or a second state value for the total.
lessons.mistake: Incorrect: store total independently and update it in several handlers. Correct: calculate total from price and quantity.
lessons.exercise: Add a discountPercent prop and derive the final amount. Independently explain which component should own a cart quantity shared by two views.

title: State and Events
analogy: Each render is a photograph of state. Event handlers belong to that photograph; setters request the next photograph.

lessons.title: Respond to events with state

notes.title: useState
notes.text: The Hook returns the current value and a setter. Initial state is used on mount. A setter requests another render; it does not mutate the current render snapshot.

notes.title: Event handlers
notes.text: Pass a function, such as onClick={increment}. Writing onClick={increment()} runs it during rendering. Events are a good place for user-triggered side effects.

notes.title: Controlled inputs
notes.text: A text input with value and onChange follows React state. Initialize it to an empty string rather than switching between undefined and a string.

lessons.output: The greeting follows the input as you type.
lessons.why: State connects user interaction to a recalculated view.
lessons.internals: React retains state between renders at a component position. Calling setName queues an update; the next call to the component receives the new value.
lessons.mistake: Do not assign name = ... or manipulate the input DOM directly. Call the setter from onChange.
lessons.exercise: Add a button that clears the name. Independently reject names over 30 characters using an input constraint.
lessons.question: What should onClick normally receive?
options: The result of calling a handler during render

lessons.title: Queue immutable updates

notes.title: Functional state updates
notes.text: Use setCount(previous => previous + 1) when computing from previous state. It composes correctly with other queued updates.

notes.title: Batching
notes.text: React groups many state updates before rendering. Reading a variable after its setter still reads the current render snapshot. Do not rely on a synchronous DOM update.

notes.title: Object and array state
notes.text: Copy every changed path. Use map to replace one item, filter to remove, and spread to append. Copying only the array does not copy its objects.

notes.title: Avoiding direct state mutation
notes.text: Mutation can hide changes and corrupt earlier snapshots. Keep updater functions pure; development checks may call them more than once.

lessons.output: Each click increases the count by 2.
lessons.why: Updater functions express a change relative to the pending state rather than a stale captured value.
lessons.internals: React applies queued updater functions in sequence. Each receives the result of the previous updater.
lessons.mistake: Incorrect: two setCount(count + 1) calls usually replace with the same number. Correct: queue two functional increments.
lessons.exercise: Add three using three updaters. Independently toggle one todo without modifying its original object.
lessons.question: Two functional +1 updates from 0 produce which value?

lessons.title: Lift, derive, preserve, and reset

notes.title: Lifting state up
notes.text: Move shared state to the closest common parent and pass values and callbacks down. Avoid a global store for data used by only two sibling components.

notes.title: Derived state
notes.text: Calculate filtered lists, totals, and validation flags during render when inexpensive. Store inputs, not every result.

notes.title: State preservation and reset
notes.text: React preserves state for the same component type and key at the same tree position. Changing a key deliberately starts a new component identity.

notes.title: State updates and rendering
notes.text: Rendering calculates output; committing applies necessary DOM changes. A render does not imply that every DOM node changed.

lessons.output: Typing changes the draft. Reset draft remounts the editor and clears it.
lessons.why: Correct ownership reduces synchronization code and makes resets intentional.
lessons.internals: A new key causes React to unmount the old editor and mount a new one, including resetting its Hook state and Effects.
lessons.mistake: Avoid random keys: they reset state on every render. Use stable identity except when a full reset is intentional.
lessons.exercise: Build two inputs sharing one value in their parent. Independently reset only one draft using a stable version key.
lessons.question: What can deliberately reset a component subtree?

title: Lists and Conditional UI
analogy: A key is a student ID, not their seat number. Students can move seats without changing identity.

lessons.title: Render stable collections

notes.title: map and list rendering
notes.text: Transform records into elements with map. Keep data objects separate from presentation and include a useful empty state.

notes.title: Stable keys
notes.text: Use a persistent domain ID unique among siblings. Keys help React match items between renders; they are not passed as ordinary props.

notes.title: Filtering and sorting
notes.text: Filter then sort a copied array. Never sort source state in place. Stable IDs preserve input state when items are reordered.

lessons.output: Asha followed by Zoya.
lessons.why: Stable identity prevents subtle bugs when a list contains stateful rows.
lessons.internals: Reconciliation matches siblings by key and type. Index keys represent position, so insertion can associate old state with a different record.
lessons.mistake: Incorrect: key={Math.random()} or changing array index for editable rows. Correct: use the saved record ID.
lessons.exercise: Add a filter for names containing a. Independently reorder editable rows and demonstrate why an ID key matters.
lessons.question: Which key best survives sorting?

lessons.title: Represent every data state

notes.title: Empty states
notes.text: Explain why no items appear and offer a next action. Distinguish an empty dataset from a search with no matches.

notes.title: Loading and error states
notes.text: Model loading, success, and failure explicitly. Show a retry when a failed read can be repeated safely. Announce changing status without repeatedly interrupting users.

notes.title: Conditional expressions
notes.text: Prefer clear early returns for major state branches. Nested ternaries become hard to audit; split meaningful branches into components.

lessons.output: No students match your search.
lessons.why: Explicit states prevent blank screens and ambiguous failure.
lessons.internals: Only one branch returns for each state. A status variable makes contradictory combinations less likely than several independent booleans.
lessons.mistake: Do not display No results while a request is still loading. Check pending and error conditions before empty data.
lessons.exercise: Render each branch using fixed props. Independently add a retry callback visible only on error.
lessons.question: When should an empty state appear?
options: After a successful read with no matching records

lessons.title: Search and paginate derived views

notes.title: Searchable lists
notes.text: Store the query and derive matching records. Normalize case for a simple local search; do not silently change the source records.

notes.title: Pagination fundamentals
notes.text: Use an offset of (page - 1) * pageSize. Reset or clamp the page when filters reduce the result count. Disable unavailable directions.

notes.title: Reusable list components
notes.text: Accept items and a renderItem callback, or children, when visual structure repeats. Avoid abstracting away useful semantics such as table headers.

lessons.output: ["Meera", "Zoya"]
lessons.why: Pagination makes large collections manageable without confusing the relationship between filtering and navigation.
lessons.internals: Filtering happens before slicing. Filtering only the current page would hide matching records on other pages.
lessons.mistake: Do not leave page=8 when a filter produces one page. Reset page on query changes or clamp it to the available range.
lessons.exercise: Change pageSize to 3 and predict page two. Independently implement a function returning totalPages and the requested slice.
lessons.question: What should happen when a new filter makes the current page invalid?

title: Forms and Validation
analogy: A form is a conversation: each field asks a clear question, and validation explains how to repair an answer.

lessons.title: Choose controlled or uncontrolled input

notes.title: Controlled versus uncontrolled forms
notes.text: Controlled inputs use value and onChange; uncontrolled inputs use the DOM as the value source and are read with FormData or refs. Both can be appropriate.

notes.title: Input handling
notes.text: Use checked for checkboxes and value for text/select controls. Radio buttons share a name and have distinct values. Convert numeric strings deliberately.

notes.title: Form submission
notes.text: Use a real form and submit button. preventDefault keeps a client-only demo from navigating. Read named fields with FormData when live state is unnecessary.

lessons.output: Submitting a nonempty name displays a greeting without navigating.
lessons.why: The input model should match whether the UI needs every keystroke or only submitted values.
lessons.internals: FormData reads successful named controls. Disabled controls are omitted; unchecked checkboxes are absent rather than false.
lessons.mistake: An input without a name is not included in FormData. Do not assume checkbox data is a JavaScript boolean.
lessons.exercise: Add a select for track and a checkbox for newsletter. Independently print only the submitted values without storing every keystroke.
lessons.question: Which field attribute is necessary for FormData inclusion?

lessons.title: Validate and explain errors

notes.title: Required fields
notes.text: Native required, minLength, and type=email offer useful baseline checks. Client validation improves feedback but does not replace validation by a trusted server.

notes.title: Validation and error messages
notes.text: Validate meaningful domain rules and place specific errors near fields. A user should know both what failed and how to correct it.

notes.title: Accessible forms
notes.text: Associate label and input, use aria-describedby for help, and aria-invalid when invalid. Focus the first invalid field after a custom validation failure.

notes.title: Form state
notes.text: Keep field values and submitted/touched state separate. Derive validity from values; avoid duplicating each validity result in independent state.

lessons.output: An object containing name and email errors. The email pattern is a practical demo check, not a complete email standard parser.
lessons.why: A pure validation function is easier to test than error logic scattered across event handlers.
lessons.internals: Validation computes a result from values. The UI decides when to show that result and where to move focus.
lessons.mistake: Do not communicate errors only through red borders. Include text and a programmatic association with the input.
lessons.exercise: Test blank, whitespace-only, and valid names. Independently add a minimum age rule using explicit numeric conversion.
lessons.question: Does client validation make an API input trustworthy?
options: No; validate on the trusted server too

lessons.title: Design a registration workflow

notes.title: Select, checkbox, and radio inputs
notes.text: Use select for choosing one option from a list, checkbox for independent booleans, and a fieldset of radios for a small exclusive set. Keep labels clickable.

notes.title: Multi-step forms
notes.text: Store values above step components so navigation preserves them. Validate each step before advancing and allow back navigation without discarding input.

notes.title: Practical registration form
notes.text: Collect name, email, track, and consent. Review the data before final submission. The included registration project stores a local demonstration record and creates no account.

lessons.output: A track chooser and consent checkbox; the review button is disabled until consent is checked.
lessons.why: A long form becomes easier when each step has a clear purpose and preserves prior work.
lessons.internals: Mounting and unmounting a step would reset local state, so shared values must live in a parent that stays mounted.
lessons.mistake: Do not store a checkbox using event.target.value and expect a boolean. Use event.target.checked.
lessons.exercise: Add a back button with type="button". Independently build a two-step review that preserves track and consent.
lessons.question: Where should values live when step components unmount?

title: React Hooks
analogy: An Effect is a synchronization contract with something outside React, including an agreement for disconnecting.

lessons.title: Synchronize with Effects

notes.title: Rules of Hooks
notes.text: Call ordinary Hooks unconditionally at the top level of a component or custom Hook. Stable call order lets React associate each Hook with its state. The special use API has different placement rules; it is not covered by this rule shorthand.

notes.title: useState and useEffect
notes.text: State stores UI memory. Effects synchronize committed UI with external systems such as timers, subscriptions, and browser APIs. Calculations from existing props/state usually belong in render.

notes.title: Dependency arrays
notes.text: List all reactive values used by an Effect. React compares dependencies with Object.is. [] does not mean ignore every future value; it means the Effect uses no reactive dependencies.

notes.title: Cleanup functions and Effect lifecycle
notes.text: Return cleanup to undo a subscription or timer. React cleans up old synchronization before running it for changed dependencies, and on unmount. Development StrictMode adds a setup-cleanup rehearsal.

notes.title: Beginner explanation
notes.text: An Effect connects a component to something React does not own, such as a timer. If all you need is a value calculated from props, calculate it directly.

notes.title: Intermediate explanation
notes.text: Treat setup and cleanup as one reversible operation. On a changed dependency, disconnect the old resource before connecting the new one. The dependency list describes the values used; it is not an arbitrary schedule.

notes.title: Advanced explanation
notes.text: An Effect belongs to committed UI. Development setup-cleanup repetition tests reversibility. A stale subscription after unmount is a lifetime bug, not a reason to disable development checks.

notes.title: Practical scenario and trade-off
notes.text: For a room subscription, connect using roomId and return unsubscribe. The trade-off is explicit lifecycle code, but you gain correct switching and teardown.

lessons.output: The count rises approximately once per second and the timer stops on unmount.
lessons.why: External systems do not automatically follow React component lifetimes. Effects establish and release that connection.
lessons.internals: Effects run after a commit. A functional updater avoids reading seconds inside the Effect, so the timer can stay connected without a seconds dependency.
lessons.mistake: Do not hide missing dependencies with an empty array. Change the design so the Effect expresses its real inputs.
lessons.exercise: Add a pause prop and recreate the timer only when it changes. Independently verify cleanup after mounting and unmounting the component.
lessons.question: When is Effect cleanup used?
options: Before changed synchronization and on unmount

lessons.title: Choose the appropriate Hook

notes.title: useRef
notes.text: A ref stores a mutable value that survives renders without causing rendering. Use it for DOM focus or an imperative handle, not a value the UI must display reactively.

notes.title: useContext
notes.text: Read the nearest provider value. It avoids passing values through unrelated intermediates, but updates can re-render consumers. Context is not automatically a selector-based store.

notes.title: useReducer
notes.text: A reducer groups state transitions into named actions. It must return new state without side effects. It is useful when transitions interact, but overkill for one boolean.

notes.title: useMemo and useCallback
notes.text: useMemo caches a calculated value; useCallback caches a function identity. They are performance tools, not correctness requirements. Measure and use them only when identity or expensive work matters.

lessons.output: The button moves keyboard focus into the search input.
lessons.why: Different Hooks solve different ownership and synchronization problems; using all of them is not a goal.
lessons.internals: React assigns the DOM node to the ref during commit. Updating ref.current does not enqueue a component render.
lessons.mistake: Do not use a ref instead of state for a visible score; changes will not refresh the UI. Do not memoize trivial arithmetic by habit.
lessons.exercise: Add a button that selects the input text. Independently implement a reducer with increment and reset actions.
lessons.question: Does changing ref.current schedule a render?

lessons.title: Extract and test custom Hooks

notes.title: Custom Hooks
notes.text: A use-prefixed function composes Hooks to share stateful logic. Each invocation gets independent state unless it reads a shared external source or provider.

notes.title: Stale closures
notes.text: An Effect captures values from its render. Missing dependencies can preserve an old value. Functional updaters help for previous-state calculations; they do not fix every stale input.

notes.title: Avoiding unnecessary Effects
notes.text: Calculate filtered data in render and handle a user action in its event handler. Effects are needed when synchronization must continue independently of one event.

notes.title: Hook testing
notes.text: Use renderHook for a logic-focused Hook and act for direct updates. Prefer testing a component when the actual user interaction is what matters.

notes.title: Beginner explanation
notes.text: A callback remembers the environment where it was created. It does not automatically receive every later render value.

notes.title: Intermediate explanation
notes.text: An empty dependency array can accidentally keep a callback from the first render. Functional state updates solve previous-state calculations, while changing props still need a correct synchronization design.

notes.title: Advanced explanation
notes.text: Separate reactive synchronization from nonreactive reading only when the API contract supports it. React 19.2+ useEffectEvent has a narrow Effect-oriented role; it is not a general workaround for dependency analysis.

notes.title: Practical scenario and trade-off
notes.text: For an interval increment, use the updater form. For switching a data source, include the source identity and reconnect. These are different problems even if both involve closures.

lessons.output: The button begins at 2 and increments on each click.
lessons.why: Extraction makes behavior reusable while keeping the same rules and ownership model.
lessons.internals: Two calls to useCounter create two Hook state sequences. The function shares implementation, not a singleton count.
lessons.mistake: Do not assume all users of a custom Hook share state. Use a provider or external store when shared identity is required.
lessons.exercise: Render two counters and prove independence. Independently write a renderHook test verifying reset to the initial value.
lessons.question: What do separate calls to a custom Hook normally share?

title: Component Architecture
analogy: Good component boundaries resemble departments with clear responsibilities and small, explicit handoffs.

lessons.title: Find boundaries and compose

notes.title: Component boundaries
notes.text: Split by responsibility, repeated behavior, or independently meaningful UI. Do not create a component solely because a file exceeds an arbitrary line count.

notes.title: Composition over duplication
notes.text: Extract repeated structure while keeping variable content explicit. Similar-looking components with different behavior do not always need one giant abstraction.

notes.title: Presentational and state-owning components
notes.text: A state owner coordinates data and operations; a presentational component receives a useful interface. This is a flexible design lens, not a rule forbidding state in UI components.

lessons.output: A meaningful empty state with caller-provided action.
lessons.why: A focused boundary reduces the number of reasons a component needs to change.
lessons.internals: Props describe a contract between components. Composition can keep state near its owner and avoid making a generic wrapper depend on domain-specific stores.
lessons.mistake: Do not build a UniversalCard with dozens of unrelated flags. Prefer composition when content varies independently.
lessons.exercise: Design an error panel accepting title, message, and action. Independently identify one boundary in the notes project that owns persistence.
lessons.question: What is a useful reason to extract a component?

lessons.title: Design controlled component APIs

notes.title: Reusable UI patterns
notes.text: Provide semantic defaults, support a caller label, and forward only intentional DOM props. Document disabled and error behavior.

notes.title: Controlled component APIs
notes.text: A controlled widget receives its value and emits changes through onChange. The parent remains authoritative; the child should not silently maintain a conflicting copy.

notes.title: Compound component concepts
notes.text: A group such as Tabs, TabList, and TabPanel can coordinate through Context. This improves composition but requires careful IDs, keyboard behavior, and state ownership.

lessons.output: A checkbox controlled by its parent state.
lessons.why: An explicit API allows the same widget to participate in forms, settings panels, and tests.
lessons.internals: The input emits an intent, the parent updates state, and the new prop completes the loop. This keeps programmatic resets and user changes consistent.
lessons.mistake: Avoid a child state initialized from checked unless the API intentionally supports an uncontrolled defaultChecked mode.
lessons.exercise: Add disabled support without breaking the label. Independently sketch a tabs API and explain why click-only tabs are incomplete.
lessons.question: Who owns a controlled component value?

lessons.title: Contain errors and refactor safely

notes.title: Error boundaries
notes.text: A boundary catches descendant render/lifecycle errors and renders fallback UI. It does not automatically catch event-handler errors or arbitrary async rejection. Catch those at their operation boundary.

notes.title: Feature-based folder structures
notes.text: Group related UI, data logic, and tests by feature when a project grows. Shared folders should contain actual cross-feature contracts rather than every utility.

notes.title: Refactoring large components
notes.text: Preserve behavior with tests, extract pure calculations first, then split UI and ownership. Change one boundary at a time.

lessons.output: Healthy panel; a throwing descendant would instead show the fallback.
lessons.why: An isolated failure should not necessarily erase the whole application.
lessons.internals: An error boundary participates in React render recovery. A Promise callback outside rendering has a different execution path and needs explicit rejection handling.
lessons.mistake: Do not promise that a boundary catches every error. Use try/catch in async operations and explicit validation at external boundaries.
lessons.exercise: Wrap a component that throws to test the fallback. Independently add a reset mechanism by remounting the boundary with a new key.
lessons.question: Which failure is not automatically caught by a React error boundary?

title: Routing with React Router
analogy: The URL is a shareable address for application state; nested routes are rooms inside a common building.

lessons.title: Create routes and shared layouts

notes.title: Client-side routing
notes.text: A router maps a URL to UI without a full document navigation for each internal link. A static host still needs a fallback for browser-history URLs.

notes.title: BrowserRouter and route definitions
notes.text: Wrap declarative Routes in BrowserRouter for pathname navigation. This repository defaults to HashRouter for portable static hosting; examples explain both.

notes.title: Navigation links
notes.text: Link navigates internally; NavLink can expose active styling and aria-current. Use ordinary anchors for external sites.

notes.title: Nested layouts
notes.text: A parent route renders Outlet where child content belongs. Shared navigation can remain mounted as the child route changes.

lessons.output: Home and About share navigation; clicking a Link changes the rendered page.
lessons.why: Routing makes views addressable, reloadable, and understandable through browser history.
lessons.internals: The router observes history changes, matches route definitions, and renders the selected branch. Outlet marks the insertion point for nested routes.
lessons.mistake: Do not mount another BrowserRouter inside a component already under a router. A standalone example may own one; an embedded panel should use the existing router.
lessons.exercise: Add a Contact child route. Independently configure a server fallback and reload /about directly.
lessons.question: What renders a nested route inside its parent layout?

lessons.title: Keep navigable state in the URL

notes.title: Route parameters
notes.text: A segment such as lessons/:lessonId supplies a string via useParams. Validate it and show a useful not-found state when the record does not exist.

notes.title: Search parameters
notes.text: useSearchParams reads and updates query values. Store shareable filters and page numbers here, while transient input focus belongs locally.

notes.title: Not-found pages
notes.text: A wildcard route handles unmatched paths. A matched route with a missing record still needs its own missing-record branch.

notes.title: URL-driven application state
notes.text: Use one source of truth. Derive filters from search params and update those params rather than maintaining a second divergent state.

lessons.output: Within a router, typing updates the q parameter and removes a stale page parameter.
lessons.why: A copied URL should reproduce the same meaningful filtered view.
lessons.internals: Search params are strings. Parse numeric values defensively and clamp invalid pages instead of trusting arbitrary query text.
lessons.mistake: Do not replace all parameters when editing one filter unless intentionally clearing the others. Clone and update the current URLSearchParams.
lessons.exercise: Add a technology parameter while retaining q. Independently handle a non-numeric page parameter as page 1.
lessons.question: Which state belongs naturally in a shareable URL?

lessons.title: Split routes and handle boundaries

notes.title: Protected-route concepts
notes.text: A client guard can redirect or hide UI for convenience, but it cannot enforce server authorization. A static demo must not pretend a local flag is secure authentication.

notes.title: Lazy-loaded routes
notes.text: React.lazy and Suspense defer downloading a page module until needed. Declare lazy components at module scope. The imported module must expose the expected default component.

notes.title: Route-level error handling
notes.text: Data routers support route error boundaries for loader/action failures. Declarative routers can wrap page elements in a React boundary; handle fetch failures explicitly in page state.

notes.title: Routing trade-offs
notes.text: Hash routing avoids static-host rewrite requirements; BrowserRouter provides clean paths with appropriate hosting support. Neither is universally better.

lessons.output: After creating Reports.jsx with a default export, the fallback appears until its module is available.
lessons.why: Route splitting reduces initial work for visitors who never open every page.
lessons.internals: lazy caches its import Promise and result. A rejected module import needs an error boundary; Suspense handles waiting, not all failures.
lessons.mistake: Do not claim a protected route secures an API. Verify permissions in a trusted service before returning protected data.
lessons.exercise: Create Reports.jsx and observe its separate network request. Independently add an error boundary around the Suspense region.
lessons.question: Does hiding an admin route prevent unauthorized API calls?
options: No; the server must enforce authorization
Yes, if the link is hidden
Yes, if the route is lazy

title: Context and State Management
analogy: Local state is a personal notebook; Context is a shared noticeboard; cached server data is a copy of an external record.

lessons.title: Place state deliberately

notes.title: Prop drilling
notes.text: Passing a value through many unrelated components can obscure intent. Before adding Context, consider composition that passes the needed content directly.

notes.title: Context API
notes.text: createContext defines a channel; a provider supplies a value and useContext reads the closest provider. Default values apply when no provider exists.

notes.title: When Context is appropriate
notes.text: Use it for a theme, locale, or shared feature state needed across a subtree. High-frequency broad updates may benefit from finer subscriptions.

notes.title: Local versus shared state
notes.text: Keep a field draft local unless another view must coordinate with it. Lifting everything globally increases coupling.

lessons.output: Theme: dark
lessons.why: Context solves distribution, while careful ownership still determines how values change.
lessons.internals: React finds the nearest matching provider. When its value changes, consumers reading that context can render again even if unrelated props are memoized.
lessons.mistake: Do not create a Context inside render; that creates a different channel each time. Define it at module scope.
lessons.exercise: Add a nested light provider and compare two badges. Independently keep a search draft outside the theme context.
lessons.question: Which provider value does a consumer read?

lessons.title: Combine reducers and normalized state

notes.title: useReducer with Context
notes.text: A provider can own a reducer and expose state plus dispatch. Separate contexts for state and dispatch can avoid forcing dispatch-only consumers to subscribe to state.

notes.title: State normalization
notes.text: Store entities by ID and reference them by ID from lists. Updating one record then changes one canonical object instead of several inconsistent copies.

notes.title: Reducer design
notes.text: Actions describe domain events such as task/completed. A reducer returns the next value from state and action and performs no network or storage side effects.

lessons.output: true; the original task remains unchanged.
lessons.why: Named transitions make a growing workflow inspectable and testable.
lessons.internals: A reducer computes new references along changed paths and preserves unaffected references. Normalization makes the location of a record unambiguous.
lessons.mistake: Do not call fetch or localStorage.setItem inside the reducer. Perform effects outside and dispatch their outcomes.
lessons.exercise: Add task/renamed with a title payload. Independently reject an empty title without changing the original state.
lessons.question: Which operation belongs outside a reducer?

lessons.title: Choose tools without overengineering

notes.title: Server state versus client state
notes.text: Remote data has freshness, retries, invalidation, and shared ownership concerns. A selected tab is client state. Treating both identically can create unnecessary cache logic.

notes.title: Redux Toolkit concepts
notes.text: A store contains shared state; slices define reducers and actions. Redux Toolkit uses Immer for mutation-like reducer syntax, which is not permission to mutate ordinary React state. It is discussed here, not installed.

notes.title: Lightweight state-management alternatives
notes.text: Context plus useReducer, useSyncExternalStore-based stores, and libraries such as Zustand offer different subscription and tooling trade-offs. Evaluate requirements before adding dependencies.

notes.title: Choosing the right approach
notes.text: Begin local, lift when needed, add Context for distribution, and use a server-state library for real caching requirements. Team debugging needs and update frequency matter.

notes.title: Beginner explanation
notes.text: Start by keeping state where it is used. Share it only when more than one part of the UI needs coordinated access.

notes.title: Intermediate explanation
notes.text: Context distributes a value; it does not supply request caching or automatically select a tiny part of a large state object. Server data also has freshness and invalidation needs.

notes.title: Advanced explanation
notes.text: Subscription granularity, write frequency, debugging tools, and team conventions influence store choice. Normalized entity state and a query cache may coexist, but define which is authoritative.

notes.title: Practical scenario and trade-off
notes.text: A theme fits Context; an input draft usually stays local; a remote paginated catalog fits a cache keyed by filters. Extra libraries are useful only when their policy replaces real complexity.

lessons.output: A table mapping each kind of value to a suitable owner.
lessons.why: Tools should solve observed coordination problems rather than add layers for their own sake.
lessons.internals: Context distributes a value; Redux-style stores coordinate transitions and subscriptions; query libraries also model asynchronous cache lifecycles. These are overlapping, not identical, responsibilities.
lessons.mistake: Do not store the same remote record in several independent client stores without a clear synchronization policy.
lessons.exercise: Classify five values in your capstone by ownership. Independently explain when introducing a global store would reduce complexity.
lessons.question: Which concern is characteristic of server state?

title: API Integration and Asynchronous UI
analogy: A request is a parcel in transit: it can arrive late, fail, or become irrelevant because you requested something else.

lessons.title: Build a reliable fetch boundary

notes.title: Fetch API and HTTP methods/status codes
notes.text: GET reads, POST commonly creates, PATCH partially updates, and DELETE removes according to the API contract. Check response.ok and understand 204 before parsing JSON.

notes.title: Loading, success, empty, and error states
notes.text: Represent request state explicitly. Preserve enough context for a meaningful retry. Empty successful data is not a failure.

notes.title: Async operations
notes.text: await suspends the async function, not the browser. Catch rejections where you can choose a user-facing recovery.

notes.title: API configuration using Vite environment variables
notes.text: Use a public base URL and encode dynamic path/query values. The default course fixture works locally with no service or API key.

lessons.output: Resolves to the bundled course records, or rejects with an explanatory error.
lessons.why: A small API client keeps transport details separate from presentation.
lessons.internals: fetch returns a Response first. JSON parsing is another asynchronous operation and can fail even after an HTTP success.
lessons.mistake: Do not blindly call response.json() for a 204 response or treat every resolved fetch as successful.
lessons.exercise: Load the local course fixture and show its title list. Independently test a malformed payload and a non-OK response.
lessons.question: What should you check before interpreting an HTTP response as success?

lessons.title: Cancel obsolete work and avoid races

notes.title: AbortController and request cancellation
notes.text: Create a controller for each synchronization and pass its signal to fetch. Cleanup aborts work that no longer belongs to the current view.

notes.title: Race conditions
notes.text: An earlier request can finish after a later one and overwrite fresh data. Cancellation plus an active/request-identity guard prevents stale results from committing.

notes.title: Pagination and filtering
notes.text: Include page and filters in the request identity. Reset page when query changes. Mock APIs should exercise the same visible states as remote calls.

notes.title: Mock API examples that work locally
notes.text: This repository ships fixture JSON and a Promise-based simulator with success, empty, and error modes. Simulation is clearly labeled and never presented as live data.

notes.title: Beginner explanation
notes.text: A response can arrive after you have moved on. Do not let yesterday’s question overwrite today’s answer.

notes.title: Intermediate explanation
notes.text: Associate each request with its URL or query identity. Cleanup aborts the previous request; an active flag prevents noncancelable follow-up work from publishing an obsolete result.

notes.title: Advanced explanation
notes.text: Cancellation saves resources when honored. Identity guards protect correctness even when completion cannot be prevented. For mutations, cancellation does not prove a server-side action was undone.

notes.title: Practical scenario and trade-off
notes.text: Search quickly from A to B and resolve A last in a test. The visible data must still belong to B. This is more useful than adding an arbitrary delay and hoping ordering stays favorable.

lessons.output: The Hook returns loading, then success or error; obsolete requests cannot update its state.
lessons.why: A user can change intent faster than a network response arrives.
lessons.internals: The cleanup closes over the old active flag and controller. The next Effect creates its own pair, so only its current result is allowed to commit.
lessons.mistake: Ignoring cancellation can show the wrong record after quick navigation. Do not show an abort as a user-facing failure.
lessons.exercise: Test two requests that resolve in reverse order. Independently add an error message while keeping aborts silent.
lessons.question: Why can a request-identity guard still be useful with cancellation?
options: Some async work may not honor abort

lessons.title: Cache and update with TanStack Query

notes.title: Data caching concepts
notes.text: A cache key identifies the data, including relevant filters. Freshness is a policy, not proof that remote data cannot change. Distinguish pending from background refetching.

notes.title: TanStack Query concepts and practical examples
notes.text: A QueryClientProvider supplies the cache. useQuery accepts queryKey and queryFn; the query function must reject on failure. staleTime controls freshness expectations.

notes.title: Optimistic updates
notes.text: Show a likely change before confirmation, snapshot previous cache data, and roll back on failure. Cancel conflicting reads and invalidate afterward. Use this only when reconciliation is well defined.

notes.title: Trade-offs
notes.text: Caching libraries remove repetitive async state code but introduce policies to understand. A single static fixture does not require a cache; the runnable query example exists to teach the behavior.

lessons.output: A loading message followed by the local course count; repeated mounts can use the cache.
lessons.why: Caching coordinates repeated reads across views and provides explicit invalidation after writes.
lessons.internals: Query keys address cached results. The query function receives an AbortSignal; forwarding it allows the library to cancel its underlying fetch.
lessons.mistake: Do not create a new QueryClient inside every render or omit a filter from the query key.
lessons.exercise: Add a category to the query key. Independently sketch optimistic rollback for a renamed course and explain conflicting updates.
lessons.question: What must be included in a query key when it changes the returned data?
options: A random number on each render

title: Styling and UI Systems
analogy: Design tokens are a shared vocabulary for spacing, color, and type, so every component speaks the same visual language.

lessons.title: Build responsive layouts

notes.title: Plain CSS and CSS Modules
notes.text: Plain CSS is useful for resets and tokens. CSS Modules transform class names for local scope; import styles from a .module.css file and use styles.card.

notes.title: Responsive design and mobile-first design
notes.text: Start with a usable narrow layout, then add columns when space permits. Breakpoints should follow content needs rather than device brand names.

notes.title: Flexbox and Grid
notes.text: Flexbox aligns items along one main axis. Grid describes rows and columns. Use minmax and min-width:0 to prevent long content from forcing overflow.

lessons.output: Cards use one column on narrow screens and two at 48rem or wider.
lessons.why: A layout should accommodate content and user zoom instead of assuming one screen size.
lessons.internals: Grid distributes available space between tracks; minmax(0,1fr) lets tracks shrink below the intrinsic width of long content.
lessons.mistake: Avoid a fixed desktop width on the page. Test long code, long titles, and 200% zoom as well as a typical phone width.
lessons.exercise: Build a three-card layout. Independently add a third column only when the content remains readable.
lessons.solution:
.cards { display:grid; gap:1rem; grid-template-columns:repeat(auto-fit,minmax(min(100%,16rem),1fr)); }
.card { min-width:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere; }
lessons.question: Which tool naturally describes both rows and columns?

lessons.title: Define themes and tokens

notes.title: Design tokens
notes.text: Name colors by role, such as surface and text, and spacing by a consistent scale. Components should use roles rather than scattered literal colors.

notes.title: Reusable themes and dark mode
notes.text: Override token values at a root data attribute. Respect system preference initially, allow a user override, and persist only the preference.

notes.title: Layout and typography
notes.text: Set a readable line-height and a bounded prose measure. Distinguish headings, metadata, and body text with a restrained scale rather than many font families.

lessons.output: The same components inherit a light or dark token palette.
lessons.why: Central theme values keep contrast and visual consistency manageable as a project grows.
lessons.internals: Custom properties cascade and inherit. Changing the root theme updates dependent properties without re-rendering each React component.
lessons.mistake: Do not invert every color blindly. Test text, borders, focus outlines, and disabled states in both themes.
lessons.exercise: Add a spacing token and use it on a panel. Independently persist the theme while handling unavailable storage.
lessons.solution:
try { localStorage.setItem('theme', 'dark'); } catch { /* preference remains usable in memory */ }
document.documentElement.dataset.theme = 'dark';
lessons.question: Why use semantic color tokens?
options: To change a role consistently across components

lessons.title: Choose a UI system and navigation

notes.title: Component libraries
notes.text: A library can accelerate common controls, but inspect keyboard behavior, theming, bundle cost, and maintenance. A library label alone does not guarantee accessibility.

notes.title: Utility-first CSS concepts
notes.text: Utilities compose styles through small classes. They can improve consistency with a defined scale but need conventions to avoid unreadable duplication. This repository uses plain CSS.

notes.title: Responsive navigation
notes.text: Use a real button to toggle narrow-screen navigation, connect aria-expanded and aria-controls, and retain logical keyboard order. Avoid inaccessible hover-only menus.

notes.title: Reduced decoration
notes.text: Animations should serve feedback, respect reduced motion, and avoid shifting content during loading.

lessons.output: Menu toggles the visibility and announced expanded state of the navigation.
lessons.why: A design system is behavior and conventions as well as visual styling.
lessons.internals: hidden removes the collapsed navigation from layout and normal accessibility exposure. The trigger remains available to reopen it.
lessons.mistake: Do not use an unlabeled icon as the only menu control. Do not visually hide a drawer while leaving its links unexpectedly focusable.
lessons.exercise: Close the menu after selecting a link. Independently test it using Tab, Enter, and Space only.
lessons.solution:
// Add onClick={() => setOpen(false)} to each navigation link.
// Keep the button label and aria-expanded linked to the same open state.
lessons.question: Which attribute communicates whether a menu is open?

title: Testing and Debugging
analogy: A good test is a rehearsal of an observable promise to a user, not a photograph of private implementation details.

lessons.title: Debug and test pure behavior

notes.title: Browser debugging and React DevTools
notes.text: Use breakpoints and inspect state/props at the failure. DevTools can reveal unexpected owners and renders. Record the reproduction before changing code.

notes.title: Unit testing
notes.text: Test pure calculations with boundary inputs. Avoid reimplementing the same algorithm inside the expected value.

notes.title: Vitest
notes.text: Tests use test/expect and can share Vite transforms. npm test in this repo runs once; test:watch provides an interactive development loop.

notes.title: Continuous integration
notes.text: CI installs the lockfile, checks content, lints, tests, typechecks, and builds. A passing local run is evidence for the tested cases, not universal correctness.

lessons.output: Two tests pass when run in a *.test.js file.
lessons.why: Fast targeted tests expose regressions before manual browser testing becomes expensive.
lessons.internals: Vitest executes test modules and records assertion failures. Isolated pure functions need no DOM; interaction tests use a DOM environment.
lessons.mistake: Do not assert total(...) equals a second copy of the same implementation. Choose independently reasoned expected values.
lessons.exercise: Test negative quantities according to a documented validation rule. Independently reproduce and fix one failure using a breakpoint.
lessons.question: Which assertion is most meaningful?
options: A boundary input with an independently known result
The same formula copied into expected

lessons.title: Test components through their UI

notes.title: Component testing and React Testing Library
notes.text: Render a component, find controls by role and accessible name, and interact with userEvent. Assert visible outcomes instead of internal Hook state.

notes.title: User-centric assertions
notes.text: Prefer getByRole for present elements, queryByRole for absence, and findByRole for eventual appearance. Do not add test IDs when a meaningful label exists.

notes.title: Forms and accessible interaction
notes.text: A test locating a field by label also verifies that a usable label association exists. Test invalid submission and recovery, not just the happy path.

notes.title: Integration testing
notes.text: Render a small working route/provider tree to verify collaborating components and state ownership.

lessons.output: The test passes with the matching Counter implementation and jest-dom setup.
lessons.why: The test remains valid if component internals are refactored while the user behavior stays the same.
lessons.internals: userEvent schedules realistic input sequences. Await its asynchronous operations so assertions observe the completed interaction.
lessons.mistake: Do not query a CSS class just because it is convenient. A role and name make both intent and accessibility clearer.
lessons.exercise: Write a form test for an empty email. Independently use keyboard interaction to complete the same valid submission.
lessons.question: Which query waits for an element to appear?

lessons.title: Cover async states and real-browser limits

notes.title: Mocking network requests
notes.text: Stub the API boundary or use a request interceptor so tests control success, empty, failure, and delayed responses. Restore mocks between tests.

notes.title: Accessibility testing
notes.text: Automated checks catch some defects. Keyboard traversal, focus visibility, zoom, and screen-reader review still require manual evaluation.

notes.title: End-to-end testing concepts
notes.text: A real browser checks routing, assets, and integrated workflows. DOM emulators do not reproduce layout or all platform APIs.

notes.title: Testing trade-offs
notes.text: Use many focused tests and a few critical cross-feature flows. Avoid fragile snapshots of enormous DOM trees and arbitrary sleeps.

lessons.output: The controlled failure test passes without network access.
lessons.why: Deterministic failure cases reveal recovery bugs that a reliable local network would rarely expose.
lessons.internals: A mocked boundary supplies specific outcomes. It proves handling of those outcomes, not compatibility with every real service or browser.
lessons.mistake: Do not claim an app is fully accessible because role queries pass. Do not claim visual responsiveness from jsdom tests alone.
lessons.exercise: Test an empty successful response. Independently write a manual keyboard checklist for the quiz retry workflow.
lessons.question: What needs a real browser or manual review?
options: Responsive layout and practical keyboard flow

title: TypeScript with React
analogy: Types are a design-time contract; runtime data must still show identification at the door.

lessons.title: Type props and events

notes.title: TypeScript prerequisites
notes.text: Understand JavaScript before adding static types. Type annotations disappear from the generated JavaScript. Use .tsx for files containing JSX.

notes.title: Typing component props, interfaces, and type aliases
notes.text: Both interface and type can describe object props. Use a union when alternatives differ. Prefer a focused public contract over any.

notes.title: Event types
notes.text: React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement> describes a change event; FormEvent<HTMLFormElement> describes submission. Inline handlers often infer the correct event type.

notes.title: Children and composition
notes.text: ReactNode is appropriate for arbitrary renderable children. A single required element may use ReactElement when that stronger constraint is intended.

lessons.output: A typed reusable labeled field; passing a number as value is a compile-time error.
lessons.why: Types make component contracts visible to both teammates and tooling before a user reaches the broken path.
lessons.internals: Vite strips TypeScript syntax, but stripping alone is not a full typecheck. This repository runs tsc --noEmit before its build.
lessons.mistake: Do not use any to silence a misunderstood event type. Narrow or infer the value you actually need.
lessons.exercise: Add optional disabled support. Independently type an onSubmit callback receiving validated form values.
lessons.question: Does a TypeScript type validate downloaded JSON at runtime?

lessons.title: Model state and generic collections

notes.title: Typed Hooks
notes.text: useState often infers from its initial value. Provide an explicit union or array element type when null or [] is insufficient. Type reducer actions as discriminated unions.

notes.title: Generic components
notes.text: A type parameter lets a list preserve the relationship between items, keys, and renderItem. Do not use generics when a concrete domain type is simpler.

notes.title: Discriminated unions
notes.text: Represent mutually exclusive states with a literal status field. Narrowing by status exposes only valid fields and avoids impossible combinations.

notes.title: API response types
notes.text: Treat external JSON as unknown until runtime checks establish its shape; a type assertion alone does not inspect data.

notes.title: Beginner explanation
notes.text: A union says a value can have one of several known shapes. A status field tells you which shape is present.

notes.title: Intermediate explanation
notes.text: Narrow status before reading fields that exist only on one branch. A loading state should not have to invent data just to satisfy a broad object type.

notes.title: Advanced explanation
notes.text: Static types model code assumptions. At a network boundary, data is unknown until validated; a discriminated union only becomes trustworthy after runtime checks produce it.

notes.title: Practical scenario and trade-off
notes.text: Model a request as loading, error with message, or success with data. More explicit types add initial typing work but reduce impossible combinations throughout the UI.

lessons.output: The success branch can safely read data; the error branch can safely read message.
lessons.why: A state model should prevent invalid combinations instead of asking every component to remember which booleans agree.
lessons.internals: TypeScript narrows the union after a literal equality check. This is static reasoning about control flow, not runtime validation.
lessons.mistake: Avoid { loading: boolean, error?: string, data?: T } when a union can express exactly one state.
lessons.exercise: Add an empty state to the union. Independently write a generic keyed list with getKey and renderItem props.
lessons.question: What enables narrowing in a discriminated union?

lessons.title: Migrate with strict checking

notes.title: Form types
notes.text: Define raw form values separately from validated domain values. An HTML number input supplies a string until you parse it.

notes.title: Strict mode
notes.text: TypeScript strict enables stronger checks such as strictNullChecks. It is unrelated to React StrictMode, which performs development runtime checks.

notes.title: Gradual migration from JavaScript
notes.text: Convert a small pure module, then its callers, then one feature. Keep behavior tests while adding types. allowJs can support a temporary mixed tree.

notes.title: TypeScript variant
notes.text: The StudyFlow capstone includes a strict TypeScript implementation alongside JavaScript. Both consume the same local API contract and support the same main workflow.

lessons.output: "2" becomes { seats: 2 }; blank, fractional, or negative values throw.
lessons.why: Migration works best when each type addition clarifies a boundary and keeps the application runnable.
lessons.internals: A runtime guard rejects bad values. The return type communicates the valid shape to downstream code after the check.
lessons.mistake: Do not confuse as Booking with conversion or validation. Assertions instruct the checker; they do not transform or inspect input.
lessons.exercise: Test blank and fractional seat values. Independently migrate a reducer action union without changing behavior.
lessons.question: Are TypeScript strict and React StrictMode the same feature?
options: No, one is static checking and one is runtime development checking

title: Performance Optimization
analogy: Optimization is a measured repair: find the slow queue before adding an express lane.

lessons.title: Measure rendering and place state

notes.title: How React rendering works
notes.text: A state update can cause React to call components to calculate output. A parent render normally visits its children unless a valid optimization lets React skip work.

notes.title: Render versus commit
notes.text: Rendering computes a possible tree and must stay pure. Commit applies changes and assigns refs. Concurrent rendering may restart or discard render work.

notes.title: State placement and avoiding unnecessary re-renders
notes.text: Move frequently changing state near the components that need it. Passing stable children through a stateful wrapper can also isolate updates.

notes.title: React Profiler and measuring before optimizing
notes.text: Record a real slow interaction, identify expensive commits, and repeat under comparable conditions after one change. Development timings differ from production.

notes.title: Beginner explanation
notes.text: Calling a component calculates a view. Updating the browser is a separate step. A render does not mean the whole page was redrawn.

notes.title: Intermediate explanation
notes.text: State placement determines how far a normal update travels through the component tree. Profiling identifies which work is expensive for an actual interaction.

notes.title: Advanced explanation
notes.text: Concurrent rendering can restart or discard calculations before a commit. Pure rendering makes these attempts safe. Measure comparable production behavior before claiming a performance improvement.

notes.title: Practical scenario and trade-off
notes.text: Profile typing into a large list and then move unrelated state closer to its owner. Compare the same input and dataset; do not optimize every function on principle.

lessons.output: Clicking logs a measured render duration for this environment; no universal benchmark is implied.
lessons.why: Measuring the user interaction prevents spending complexity on work that is already fast.
lessons.internals: A render can be interrupted without committing. Side effects performed during render would still have occurred, which is why purity matters.
lessons.mistake: Do not use a console.log count as a production performance benchmark. Compare measured interactions and verify perceived responsiveness.
lessons.exercise: Profile typing into a filtered list. Independently move the input state closer to that list and compare the same interaction.
lessons.question: Which phase actually applies DOM changes?

lessons.title: Understand memoization trade-offs

notes.title: React.memo
notes.text: memo may skip a component render when its props compare equal. It does not prevent renders from that component state or consumed Context.

notes.title: useMemo and useCallback trade-offs
notes.text: Memoization costs comparisons, retained memory, and dependency complexity. Fresh object/function props can defeat a memoized child. Use caching only for a measured need.

notes.title: React Compiler concepts
notes.text: The compiler can automate some memoization when configured in a supported build. It is not enabled in this repository, and pure component rules still matter.

notes.title: Avoiding unnecessary re-renders
notes.text: A stable reference is useful only when some downstream comparison uses it. It does not make an inherently expensive algorithm cheap.

notes.title: Beginner explanation
notes.text: Memoization remembers work when inputs have not changed. Remembering a value also has a cost.

notes.title: Intermediate explanation
notes.text: A freshly constructed array or callback is a new reference, even if it looks identical. Memoization helps only where a comparison or expensive calculation benefits from stable inputs.

notes.title: Advanced explanation
notes.text: A cache may be discarded, so logic must remain correct without it. Memoized components still respond to their own state and Context. Compiler-assisted caching changes the amount of manual work, not the need for pure code.

notes.title: Practical scenario and trade-off
notes.text: Cache a measured expensive selector and compare its cost with dependency checking. For simple multiplication, recomputing is generally clearer. Avoid custom comparison functions unless you can prove correctness and benefit.

lessons.output: Results can reuse its render when the memoized filtered array and other props are unchanged.
lessons.why: A cache trades repeated computation for retained work and invalidation rules.
lessons.internals: useMemo compares dependencies with Object.is. If the parent recreates items on every render, the calculation still runs. React may discard caches, so correctness must not depend on them.
lessons.mistake: Do not omit dependencies to preserve a cache. That makes output stale rather than fast.
lessons.exercise: Remove useMemo and verify identical behavior. Independently measure whether caching helps for 10 versus 10,000 records.
lessons.question: Should application correctness depend on useMemo retaining a value forever?

lessons.title: Reduce bundle, list, and network work

notes.title: Code splitting, lazy loading, and Suspense
notes.text: Split infrequently visited features with dynamic imports. Suspense provides a waiting boundary for supported resources such as lazy components; it does not automatically observe a fetch in an Effect.

notes.title: Large-list virtualization
notes.text: Render only the visible window plus overscan when DOM volume is measured as a bottleneck. Account for item heights, focus, scroll position, and screen-reader access.

notes.title: Bundle analysis
notes.text: Inspect emitted chunks and their dependency graph. Large libraries should be justified by use. A bundle size is not equivalent to load time on every device.

notes.title: Network performance
notes.text: Compress assets at hosting, size images appropriately, cache immutable assets, and avoid sequential independent requests. Measure under representative latency.

lessons.output: { start: 7, end: 18, offset: 280 }; end is exclusive. This is range math, not a complete accessible virtual list.
lessons.why: Reducing unnecessary downloaded and rendered work can outperform micro-optimizing one callback.
lessons.internals: A virtual list preserves total scroll geometry while mounting a subset. Removing a focused row requires deliberate focus handling.
lessons.mistake: Do not virtualize a small list by default or claim Suspense handles every asynchronous operation automatically.
lessons.exercise: Calculate the range at scrollTop=0. Independently design a keyboard policy before building a virtualized interactive list.
lessons.question: What does virtualization primarily reduce?

title: Accessibility and Inclusive Design
analogy: Accessible UI provides more than one way to perceive information and operate the same controls.

lessons.title: Start with semantics and keyboard

notes.title: Semantic elements
notes.text: Use buttons for actions, anchors for navigation, and headings/landmarks for document structure. Native elements include behaviors that custom div controls must recreate.

notes.title: Keyboard navigation
notes.text: Every action must be reachable and usable without a pointer. Preserve logical DOM order, visible focus, and expected Enter/Space behavior.

notes.title: Focus management
notes.text: Move focus intentionally after navigation or a dialog transition. Avoid stealing focus on every render. The user should understand where they are.

notes.title: Screen-reader considerations
notes.text: A visible label and a programmatic accessible name should agree. Use live regions for meaningful changing status, not every keystroke.

lessons.output: Keyboard users can reach a skip link, navigation, and a native print button.
lessons.why: Keyboard and semantic support improve usability across assistive technologies and input methods.
lessons.internals: The DOM order informs sequential focus navigation and the accessibility tree. CSS visual rearrangement does not automatically change that order.
lessons.mistake: Avoid positive tabIndex values that impose a separate confusing order. Prefer native order and tabIndex=0 only where necessary.
lessons.exercise: Navigate the page without a mouse. Independently add a visible :focus-visible outline and verify it on every action.
lessons.solution:
:focus-visible { outline: 3px solid #14634e; outline-offset: 4px; }
/* Keep sufficient contrast against both adjacent colors. */
lessons.question: Which is normally best for an action?
options: A clickable span without keyboard support

lessons.title: Make forms and dialogs understandable

notes.title: Accessible forms, labels, and descriptions
notes.text: A label identifies the field; a description adds instructions or errors. Use fieldset and legend for related controls. Never rely on placeholder text as the sole label.

notes.title: Dialog accessibility
notes.text: A modal needs a name, focus placement, containment, Escape handling, background inertness, and focus restoration. Native dialog.showModal provides much of the platform behavior; test it in browsers.

notes.title: ARIA fundamentals
notes.text: ARIA changes accessibility semantics, not native interaction behavior. Prefer native elements; add ARIA only when it expresses missing state or relationships.

lessons.output: A labeled email field whose helper text is programmatically associated with it.
lessons.why: Users need to identify both a control and the instruction needed to use it correctly.
lessons.internals: aria-describedby references another element by ID. An error can replace its text while preserving the relationship.
lessons.mistake: Do not add role="button" to a div and assume keyboard behavior is solved. Do not implement a visual modal without focus handling.
lessons.exercise: Add a password helper without asking users to submit real credentials. Independently test a native dialog for Escape and restored trigger focus.
lessons.question: What does aria-describedby provide?

lessons.title: Verify contrast, motion, and usability

notes.title: Color contrast
notes.text: Normal text generally needs at least 4.5:1 under WCAG AA; large text has a 3:1 threshold. Focus indicators and controls also need careful contrast. Do not use color alone to signal state.

notes.title: Reduced motion
notes.text: Honor prefers-reduced-motion and avoid essential information conveyed only by animation. Keep transitions restrained and disable nonessential movement when requested.

notes.title: Automated and manual accessibility testing
notes.text: Use semantic queries and automated audits, then test keyboard, zoom, screen readers, error recovery, and real devices. Automated results are a subset of accessibility evidence.

notes.title: Inclusive design trade-offs
notes.text: A technically valid widget can still be hard to understand. Plain labels, short forms, and predictable navigation reduce cognitive burden.

lessons.output: Nonessential CSS animation and transitions are disabled when reduced motion is requested.
lessons.why: Accessibility must be verified in the actual experience rather than inferred from a component checklist.
lessons.internals: Media queries respond to user preferences. CSS changes motion, while labels and interaction semantics still need appropriate HTML and behavior.
lessons.mistake: Do not claim compliance from a color palette alone. Evaluate complete pages, focus order, error messages, and content at zoom.
lessons.exercise: Check the quiz at 200% zoom and with keyboard only. Independently record one manual finding and its reproducible fix.
lessons.solution:
