const audit = ['Text zoom does not hide actions', 'Errors are described in text', 'Focus is visible', 'Status uses text plus color', 'Motion respects preference'];
console.table(audit);
lessons.question: Can an automated audit prove all accessibility requirements are satisfied?

title: Security and Reliability
analogy: A browser is a public display case: anything shipped to it can be inspected and changed by its visitor.

lessons.title: Render untrusted content safely

notes.title: XSS fundamentals
notes.text: Cross-site scripting runs attacker-controlled script in another user context. It can arise from unsafe HTML, unsafe URLs, or compromised dependencies.

notes.title: Safe rendering
notes.text: React escapes ordinary text children. Rendering a user string inside JSX text does not interpret it as markup. Context still matters: URLs and raw HTML need their own validation.

notes.title: Avoiding unsafe HTML injection
notes.text: dangerouslySetInnerHTML bypasses text escaping. If rich HTML is unavoidable, use a maintained sanitizer with a clear policy and test dangerous cases. This site disables raw Markdown HTML.

lessons.output: The suspicious markup is displayed as text; it is not executed as an image event handler.
lessons.why: Content must remain data unless a deliberate, validated feature requires interpreting it.
lessons.internals: React DOM creates text nodes for ordinary string children. Bypassing that path with raw HTML changes the trust boundary.
lessons.mistake: Incorrect: inject an arbitrary comment with dangerouslySetInnerHTML. Correct: render it as text, or sanitize a constrained rich-text format.
lessons.exercise: Render a comment containing angle brackets. Independently restrict a link to approved http/https protocols.
lessons.question: How should ordinary user comments be rendered?
options: As raw injected HTML by default

lessons.title: Understand identity and secret boundaries

notes.title: Secure authentication concepts
notes.text: Authentication establishes identity through a trusted service; authorization decides allowed operations. A frontend can present the result but cannot be the sole authority.

notes.title: Token storage trade-offs
notes.text: JavaScript-accessible storage is exposed to XSS. HttpOnly cookies reduce script access but require careful CSRF, same-site, and deployment design. No one storage choice solves every threat.

notes.title: Environment-variable limitations and why VITE_ variables are public
notes.text: Vite substitutes values into client code at build time. An .env filename does not encrypt anything. Private keys belong in trusted infrastructure.

notes.title: Client-side authorization limitations
notes.text: Hiding a button or editing a route guard changes UX only. A server must check permissions on every protected request. This static course intentionally has no real login.

lessons.output: A public title is displayed; no authentication or secret is implied.
lessons.why: Understanding trust boundaries prevents a polished interface from being mistaken for a secure service.
lessons.internals: Users control their browser, localStorage, and network requests. Code shipped to that browser cannot prevent them from editing client state.
lessons.mistake: Do not store real credentials in demo forms or place a private service token in a VITE_ variable.
lessons.exercise: Inspect the built bundle for a public config value. Independently draw the trusted boundary for a hypothetical authenticated API.
lessons.question: Where must access to protected server data be enforced?
options: Only in a React route guard

lessons.title: Maintain dependencies and recover from failure

notes.title: Dependency hygiene
notes.text: Pin direct versions and retain the lockfile, inspect install changes, audit dependencies, and update deliberately. Audit output is advisory evidence, not proof of safety.

notes.title: Error handling
notes.text: Catch errors at meaningful boundaries and present recovery actions. Avoid swallowing failures silently or logging sensitive request payloads.

notes.title: Avoiding secret exposure
notes.text: Ignore private .env files, review diffs, and rotate exposed credentials. Removing a key from the latest commit does not erase prior exposure.

notes.title: Reliability
notes.text: Handle unavailable storage, malformed persisted data, failed requests, and missing records. Keep user work when a recoverable operation fails.

lessons.output: Returns saved JSON when readable, otherwise a safe fallback. Validate the parsed shape before trusting it.
lessons.why: Failures are routine conditions, so recovery needs to be part of the design.
lessons.internals: Storage access can throw because of browser policy or capacity. JSON parsing can fail independently; a successful parse can still have the wrong schema.
lessons.mistake: Do not assume try/catch plus JSON.parse validates the content. Check expected types and allowed IDs after reading.
lessons.exercise: Corrupt a saved progress value and verify recovery. Independently show an in-memory-only notice when writes fail.
lessons.question: Does a clean dependency audit guarantee an application is secure?

title: Advanced React Concepts
analogy: Concurrent rendering is interruptible planning before committing a result; it is not two threads editing the same DOM at once.

lessons.title: Understand identity and concurrent work

notes.title: Reconciliation
notes.text: React compares element descriptions and determines which mounted components and DOM nodes can be retained. Stable type, position, and keys guide identity.

notes.title: Keys and component identity
notes.text: A changed key starts a new component identity and resets its state. Keys need uniqueness among siblings, not across the entire application.

notes.title: Concurrent rendering concepts
notes.text: React can prioritize updates and interrupt work before commit. Rendering must be pure because an attempt may never be committed.

notes.title: Transitions and useTransition
notes.text: Mark a nonurgent update as a transition while keeping urgent controlled input state immediate. isPending can indicate background work. Transitions do not make expensive JavaScript run off-thread.

notes.title: Beginner explanation
notes.text: Urgent typing should not wait behind a less urgent result view. A transition marks that distinction for React.

notes.title: Intermediate explanation
notes.text: Keep controlled input state immediate and transition the dependent result state. The update may be interrupted by another urgent interaction before it commits.

notes.title: Advanced explanation
notes.text: Transition callbacks still execute on the JavaScript thread. Expensive non-React computation may need a worker or chunking; scheduling priority is not parallel execution.

notes.title: Practical scenario and trade-off
notes.text: Use a large results panel as the demonstration. A tiny label may finish too quickly for isPending to be visible. Report measured responsiveness rather than promising speed from one Hook.

lessons.output: Input updates urgently; the results state is marked nonurgent. A tiny example may not visibly remain pending.
lessons.why: Priority lets React keep urgent interactions responsive while less urgent rendering catches up.
lessons.internals: startTransition marks updates scheduled within its scope. It does not move a synchronous filtering loop into a worker or delay the callback itself.
lessons.mistake: Do not put the controlled input value update inside a transition. Keep the input immediate and transition the dependent view.
lessons.exercise: Add a measured expensive result component. Independently explain why a heavy loop inside the handler still blocks input.
lessons.question: Does startTransition move arbitrary JavaScript to another thread?

lessons.title: Defer values and locate Suspense boundaries

notes.title: useDeferredValue
notes.text: Let a derived view lag behind an urgent value. It is not a debounce timer and does not by itself reduce network requests. A memoized slow subtree may be necessary to benefit.

notes.title: Suspense boundaries
notes.text: A boundary displays fallback when descendants suspend through supported mechanisms. Place boundaries around meaningful loading regions rather than hiding an entire page for one small panel.

notes.title: Server rendering concepts and hydration
notes.text: SSR generates initial HTML on a server. Hydration attaches React behavior to matching server markup. A plain Vite client root uses createRoot, not hydration, unless you build SSR infrastructure.

notes.title: Mismatch prevention
notes.text: Server and client initial output must agree. Random values, locale differences, and current time can create mismatches when rendered independently.

notes.title: Beginner explanation
notes.text: Deferral lets a result view temporarily use an older value while an input stays current. Hydration is a different concept: it attaches behavior to server-produced HTML.

notes.title: Intermediate explanation
notes.text: Suspense waits for supported suspending resources, such as a lazy component. An ordinary Effect fetch with explicit loading state does not automatically become a Suspense resource.

notes.title: Advanced explanation
notes.text: Server and client initial trees must match for hydration. Time, random values, and differing locale defaults can violate that contract. A client-only Vite build uses createRoot and has no server markup to hydrate.

notes.title: Practical scenario and trade-off
notes.text: Choose boundaries around independently useful panels. Too broad a fallback can hide working content; too many tiny boundaries can make the experience visually fragmented.

lessons.output: The results value may briefly lag behind input; no fixed delay or request cancellation is implied.
lessons.why: Different parts of a view can have different urgency and loading boundaries.
lessons.internals: Deferred rendering allows React to retry lower-priority work. Hydration is a separate process that expects preexisting compatible server-rendered markup.
lessons.mistake: Do not use hydrateRoot on an empty root because the word sounds faster. Use createRoot for this client-only application.
lessons.exercise: Explain the distinction between deferral and debouncing. Independently identify a sensible Suspense boundary for a dashboard chart.
lessons.question: Does useDeferredValue guarantee a fixed millisecond delay?

lessons.title: Separate core APIs from infrastructure

notes.title: Server Components versus client components
notes.text: Server Components execute in a server-capable build/runtime and may access server resources. Client components support interactive state. A plain Vite SPA does not become an RSC app by adding a directive.

notes.title: Framework integration
notes.text: Frameworks can supply routing, server rendering, data loading, and RSC infrastructure. These capabilities require a compatible integration and deployment model, not just React imports.

notes.title: React Compiler concepts
notes.text: Compiler-assisted memoization requires build configuration and compatible code. This course leaves it off so the basic rendering model remains explicit.

notes.title: Current React APIs and limitations
notes.text: The installed React 19.3 line includes stable ViewTransition and Fragment refs. Their browser/platform constraints still matter. useEffectEvent from 19.2 is for nonreactive Effect logic, not a dependency-lint escape hatch. useActionState/useOptimistic support action-oriented UI; a trusted server is still required for real server mutations.

notes.title: Beginner explanation
notes.text: React APIs and a complete deployment framework are different layers. Installing React does not create a server runtime.

notes.title: Intermediate explanation
notes.text: A compatible framework can coordinate server modules, client bundles, requests, and hydration. A directive has meaning only when the build/runtime integration interprets it.

notes.title: Advanced explanation
notes.text: React 19.3 stabilizes ViewTransition and Fragment refs, but each still has platform constraints. The compiler needs configuration. Server Components need server-aware tooling and operational boundaries.

notes.title: Practical scenario and trade-off
notes.text: Use the included client-side ViewTransition example on a supported browser, and document SSR/RSC as a separate architecture decision. Do not silently add a backend just to demonstrate a conceptual distinction.

lessons.output: The details toggle works; supported browsers can animate the transition. Respect reduced-motion preferences.
lessons.why: Version and infrastructure boundaries keep learners from expecting unavailable behavior in a client-only starter.
lessons.internals: React 19.3 coordinates ViewTransition with browser capabilities. Server rendering and RSC need a separate server-aware module and execution model.
lessons.mistake: Do not teach ViewTransition as experimental for the pinned 19.3 release, or claim that this Vite SPA supports Server Components out of the box.

title: Production-Ready Applications
analogy: A release is a reproducible package plus instructions for where requests and failures should go.

lessons.title: Build and validate the release

notes.title: Environment configuration
notes.text: Separate public deployment configuration from private runtime secrets. Rebuild when public Vite configuration changes. Use a documented BASE_URL for subpath assets.

notes.title: Production builds and build validation
notes.text: Build from a clean lockfile install, serve dist, and exercise direct navigation and core workflows. Development success alone does not prove production asset resolution.

notes.title: Asset optimization and lazy loading
notes.text: Keep assets local where feasible, use appropriate formats/sizes, and split infrequent routes. Verify the emitted files rather than assuming a tool removed all unused code.

notes.title: Error handling and logging concepts
notes.text: Use boundaries and recoverable error states. Real telemetry requires a destination and a privacy policy; this local course logs no remote user analytics.

lessons.code:
npm ci
npm run content:check
npm run lint
npm test
npm run build
npm run preview
lessons.output: Each command must exit successfully before treating the candidate as verified. Build writes dist.
lessons.why: The release process needs repeatable evidence that the delivered files match the source and documentation.
lessons.internals: Build resolves imports and emits chunks. Preview serves the result; missing lazy assets may only be noticed when a specific route is opened.
lessons.mistake: Do not claim success from a build log while ignoring failing tests or broken deep links. Record the exact checks executed.

lessons.title: Deploy to static hosts

notes.title: Deployment to static hosting
notes.text: Upload dist to a static host and use the documented base path. This repository includes Netlify and Vercel configuration files and an opt-in GitHub Pages workflow.

notes.title: SPA route fallback configuration
notes.text: BrowserRouter requires unknown application paths to return index.html. HashRouter keeps routing after #, so the host receives only the actual document path.

notes.title: GitHub Pages deployment considerations
notes.text: Repository Pages often use /repo-name/. Set VITE_BASE_PATH during build, retain hash routing, and enable Pages with GitHub Actions. GitHub Pages does not provide arbitrary SPA rewrites.

notes.title: Netlify and Vercel deployment
notes.text: Use npm ci as install, npm run build as build, and dist as output. Included rewrite rules support browser routing. Select project root correctly.

lessons.output: The base path governs asset URLs; the router mode governs navigation URLs. They solve different problems.
lessons.why: A route working after clicking can still fail on direct reload if hosting cannot resolve its pathname.
lessons.internals: The URL fragment is not sent to the server. Pathnames are, so browser-history routes depend on server fallback behavior.
lessons.mistake: Do not set a repository base path on a root-domain deployment by habit, or forget it for repository Pages assets.
lessons.exercise: Build once with a /course/ base path. Independently explain which network requests should include that prefix.

$env:VITE_BASE_PATH='/react-vite-complete-course/'
npm.cmd run build
# Afterward remove the override when no longer needed:
Remove-Item Env:VITE_BASE_PATH

lessons.title: Prepare a maintainable release

notes.title: CI workflows
notes.text: The included workflow checks source on pull requests and pushes. Permissions are minimal; Pages deployment is a separate opt-in manual workflow.

notes.title: Dependency auditing
notes.text: Inspect npm audit output and assess actual exposure before upgrading. Avoid blind force-upgrades across major versions; rerun validation after updates.

notes.title: Release preparation
notes.text: Update the changelog, review the license, record versions and verification results, and exclude generated secrets, node_modules, and local user data from source archives.

notes.title: README and documentation quality
notes.text: Commands, paths, counts, and status must match reality. Content checks verify chapter metadata and local links; humans still review teaching accuracy.

lessons.code:
npm audit
npm ls --depth=0
npm run verify
npm run format:check
lessons.output: Audit and version output provide review evidence; verify and formatting checks report actual pass/fail status.
lessons.why: An open-source release needs reproducible setup and honest status as much as working UI.
lessons.internals: A lockfile records resolved transitive dependencies. CI uses npm ci to reproduce that dependency graph for its operating system.
lessons.mistake: Do not add an invented passing badge or claim full coverage without measured results. Keep limits in the implementation report.
lessons.exercise: Review the release checklist in docs. Independently propose one small dependency update with its observed validation results.

title: Architecture and Industry Practices
analogy: Architecture is a set of reversible decisions that keeps the next change understandable.

lessons.title: Organize by features and boundaries

notes.title: Feature-based architecture
notes.text: Group a feature UI, state, API adapter, and tests where ownership is clear. Promote modules to shared only when multiple features need the same stable contract.

notes.title: Separation of concerns
notes.text: Keep rendering, transport, domain validation, and persistence distinguishable. Small apps can use simple files; separation does not require many layers.

notes.title: Reusable abstractions
notes.text: Extract repeated knowledge, not merely similar syntax. A useful abstraction removes inconsistency without hiding essential behavior.

notes.title: API client organization
notes.text: Centralize transport checks, base URLs, cancellation, and response parsing. Feature adapters translate transport data into domain shapes.

lessons.output: The transport helper and feature adapter have distinct responsibilities.
lessons.why: A clear boundary limits how far a transport or UI change needs to spread.
lessons.internals: The call graph separates a generic HTTP policy from domain interpretation. Dependency direction is explicit and easy to replace in tests.
lessons.mistake: Do not create generic helpers that silently swallow all errors or know every feature shape.
lessons.exercise: Extract one API adapter from a component. Independently test it with an injected fetcher or mocked boundary.
lessons.question: What should a shared transport helper avoid owning?

lessons.title: Review forms, design systems, and changes

notes.title: Form and validation architecture
notes.text: Keep raw values, validation, submission state, and UI feedback clear. Reuse domain validators across forms with the same rules, not one massive validator for unrelated domains.

notes.title: Design systems
notes.text: Define tokens, semantic primitives, interaction states, and examples. Document keyboard behavior and error cases alongside visual variants.

notes.title: Maintainable naming conventions
notes.text: Use names that reveal domain meaning and units, such as priceCents and selectedCourseId. Avoid vague data2 or magic flags.

notes.title: Code reviews, Git branching, and pull requests
notes.text: A focused branch and PR should explain the user problem, behavior change, and evidence. Review correctness, clarity, accessibility, and recovery paths.

lessons.output: A validation error object keyed by fields with explicit units.
lessons.why: Names and review evidence help another developer reason without reconstructing every hidden assumption.
lessons.internals: Pure validation separates domain rules from when a UI chooses to reveal errors. Tests can exercise boundary values without mounting a page.
lessons.mistake: Do not mix a refactor, dependency overhaul, and unrelated visual redesign into one hard-to-review change.
lessons.exercise: Write a PR description for one form improvement. Independently include a failing case, corrected behavior, and actual test command.
lessons.question: Which variable name communicates its unit?

lessons.title: Refactor and reason about systems

notes.title: Refactoring legacy components
notes.text: Characterize behavior with tests, isolate side effects, and replace one boundary at a time. Preserve working behavior before adding new features.

notes.title: Frontend system design
notes.text: Discuss routes, state ownership, cache freshness, network failure, access boundaries, accessibility, loading performance, and observability. Draw a data-flow model before choosing libraries.

notes.title: Trade-offs and architectural decisions
notes.text: Record the problem, constraints, chosen option, alternatives, and consequences. Revisit decisions when evidence or requirements change.

notes.title: Capstone preparation
notes.text: StudyFlow combines routing, forms, a reducer, a local API, persistence, tests, and a TypeScript variant. Its scope is a complete local learning planner, not a hosted multi-tenant LMS.

lessons.output: A compact decision record with a concrete reason and revisit condition.
lessons.why: Good engineering explains why a choice fits the current constraints and what would change it.
lessons.internals: A dependency graph and state-ownership map expose coupling. Replacing one well-defined boundary is safer than rewriting an entire app at once.
lessons.mistake: Do not describe a stack as universally best. Explain its trade-offs against actual use cases and team constraints.
lessons.exercise: Write an architecture decision for local progress storage. Independently design a future sync boundary without implementing fake authentication.
lessons.question: When should an architecture decision be revisited?
